video_title: The CLARITY Act Failed. What Happens to Crypto Now?
gist: Windrock Wealth Management's Brett explains why the Clarity Act died in Congress -- ethics concerns around the Trump administration's crypto ties and an unresolved bank-vs-stablecoin fight over interest-paying deposits -- and argues the SEC and CFTC are already using no-action relief to push tokenization and near-24/7 equity trading forward regardless, while framing stablecoins as a dollar-reinforcing transactional layer that will also underpin autonomous AI-agent commerce.

insights.claim: Bitcoin follows a historical four-year 'having' cycle in which its new-issuance rate is cut in half, and that pattern has typically produced a price high within about 18 months of the having followed by a brutal roughly 12-month drawdown period.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Useful timing lens for entries/exits, though the speaker caveats that no two cycles are identical and this is not investment advice.
insights.quote: maybe the high is hit within 18 months of that. And then look out for a nasty 12-month period

insights.claim: Bitcoin fell from roughly $120,000 last fall to about $58,000 this past summer and has since rallied back to around $85,000, which the speaker frames as a good long-term entry point on a cyclical view.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the magnitude of the recent drawdown-and-recovery, giving a concrete reference range for where Bitcoin sits in its cycle.
insights.quote: we got to 120,000 last fall. We got as low as 58,000 plus or minus this summer.

insights.claim: There is a real possibility, though not a certainty, of one more washout in Bitcoin later this fall that would mark the cycle's final bottom before a more constructive multi-year stretch.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Investors sizing new crypto positions may want to watch for a final capitulation leg this fall rather than assuming the bottom is already in.
insights.quote: some people think there could be one more wash out later this fall that marks a bottom

insights.claim: The Clarity Act, which would have codified whether each crypto token is regulated as an SEC security or a CFTC commodity, failed to advance in Congress despite having had broad bipartisan support in the House a year earlier, falling short of the votes needed to continue debate.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Signals that federal crypto market-structure legislation remains stalled despite earlier momentum, keeping regulatory uncertainty elevated for token issuers and exchanges.
insights.quote: this act, which by the way had broad bipartisan support from the House a year ago, um you know, people had high hopes for it and it was really dead on arrival.

insights.claim: A key reason the Clarity Act stalled was an ethics fight over the Trump administration's personal involvement in crypto ventures, including Trump-branded coins, which turned crypto regulation into a more partisan political issue.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Political/ethics overhang tied to administration officials' personal crypto involvement could keep resurfacing as a blocker for future crypto legislation independent of the policy's underlying merits.
insights.quote: ethics maybe pointed towards Trump administration on uh participation in different cryptocurrency things.

insights.claim: The bigger sticking point on the Clarity Act was whether stablecoins can pay yield: banks lobbied hard against it because if stablecoin issuers can pay depositors more interest than banks do, deposits could flee the banking system, and bank and stablecoin lobby groups have not found a compromise.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: The deposit-flight risk to banks is the structural reason stablecoin-yield legislation keeps stalling; watch bank lobbying versus fintech/crypto lobbying as the swing factor for any future bill.
insights.quote: if stable coins can pay all of this interest and we're only paying a fraction of that, all the money is going to leave the banks and that's a banking risk.

insights.claim: Senator Tillis voted no on the Clarity Act as a procedural move that preserves his ability to bring the bill back for reconsideration, suggesting the legislation could resurface as soon as next year.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: The bill is not dead, just stalled procedurally -- worth monitoring Tillis and Senate leadership for a reintroduction timeline.
insights.quote: one of the senators, Senator Tillis, voted no but was really a yes. And that no preserves the right to bring it back up again when the climate's right.

insights.claim: Just two days after the Clarity Act stalled, the SEC and CFTC each issued their own regulatory findings, including an SEC five-year exemption for exchanges working with tokenized assets, effectively letting regulators push tokenization forward administratively without new legislation.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Regulatory relief is advancing tokenization even without a federal law, reducing the near-term dependence on Congress passing new crypto legislation.
insights.quote: two days after um the stall out of the Clarity Act, you had both the SEC and the CFTC... coming out with their own regulatory findings... they're basically giving a five-year exemption uh for exchanges working with tokenized assets.

insights.claim: The SEC/CFTC no-action stance is expected to open the door for banks and brokerages to tokenize real-world assets -- for example selling fractional, instantly-settled blockchain shares of a stock like Apple -- collapsing the traditional multi-day settlement cycle into an immediate blockchain transaction.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Watch brokerages and exchanges for tokenized-equity product launches; instant settlement could compress businesses built around T+2 settlement and financing.
insights.quote: you want to put a dollar in Apple stock? Well, we can sell you a little fraction because now Apple stock is also represented on the blockchain as a cryptocurrency and we can do it in micro fractions.

insights.claim: The New York Stock Exchange and NASDAQ are moving toward near-continuous trading, roughly a 23-hour trading day at least five days a week, pushing US equity markets toward the always-on model crypto markets already operate under.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Extended trading hours change how volatility, news reaction, and liquidity provision work in equities -- relevant for market-makers, algos, and retail trading platforms.
insights.quote: the New York Stock Exchange, NASDAQ, they're all moving forward with the idea of almost all day and night trading. More like a 23-hour trading day at least five days a week.

insights.claim: Guest Tom Lee, chairman of an Ethereum holding company, says Robinhood's Vlad Tenev and BlackRock's Larry Fink have both stated they believe the entire financial system will ultimately be rebuilt on blockchain rails.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Two of the most influential figures in brokerage and asset management on record predicting a full migration of financial infrastructure to blockchain rails is a signal worth tracking for institutional product roadmaps.
insights.quote: Vlad Tennv has made that very unequivocal statement. He thinks the entire financial system is going to be built on blockchain rails. Larry Frink at Black Rockck has said the same thing.

themes.theme: Stablecoins, the Dollar, and AI Agents

insights.claim: Stablecoins function more like a checking account -- transactional and value-stable, not meant to appreciate -- while Bitcoin and Ethereum behave more like volatile, long-term store-of-value or utility assets, meaning investors should stop treating 'crypto' as one asset class and instead segment by function.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction should differ by segment -- stablecoin holdings should be sized like cash management, not like a growth bet.
insights.quote: stable coins are going to be for transactional things where you don't want the value to fluctuate... I think it's more of a transactional utility, so to speak.

insights.claim: Rather than being purely a competitive threat to the US dollar, dollar-pegged stablecoins actually reinforce and extend the dollar's dominance by creating global demand -- especially in countries with weaker local currencies -- for dollar exposure and short-term Treasuries, even amid ongoing US fiscal stress.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth could become a structural source of foreign demand for short-dated US Treasuries -- a bullish offset to dollar-debasement worries, trackable via stablecoin market-cap growth and issuer Treasury holdings.
insights.quote: this whole stable coin framework is part of a plan I believe to help elongate the life of the dollar and some of the stresses they're feeling with the bond markets.

insights.claim: AI agents are expected to become major autonomous economic actors that transact via crypto wallets and stablecoin rails rather than traditional bank accounts -- which take days to open -- handling tasks like booking travel or making payments on a person's behalf.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: A non-obvious secular demand driver for stablecoin payment infrastructure independent of retail crypto speculation -- watch stablecoin issuers and agentic-commerce plays.
insights.quote: AI agents are going to be controlling a lot of commerce in the future... they're not going to go through a process of opening a bank account for 3 days. They are going to go on the rails of cryptocurrencies and stable coins.

insights.claim: Of the tens of thousands of existing cryptocurrencies, an estimated 95% will likely end up worthless while perhaps 5% could be 'society changing,' so the recommended approach is concentrating in networks with proven adoption -- mainly Bitcoin and Ethereum, plus a curated basket -- rather than chasing hundreds of small tokens.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: A power-law framework for token selection that favors concentration over broad diversification across the long tail of tokens.
insights.quote: I still believe that probably 95% of it will end up with no value, but 5% might be society changing, right?

insights.claim: Retail investors have historically bought crypto near cycle hype peaks and capitulated near cycle lows, which is why institutional adoption has tended to track the boom-bust cycle rather than rise steadily, and why having an advisor or institution to counteract emotional decision-making has been a differentiator this cycle.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: Retail versus institutional positioning and sentiment can serve as a contrarian timing signal for crypto allocation decisions.
insights.quote: the retail investor unfortunately they buy in when the hype is at its highest and price is maybe fully reflective of that. And then when it washes out like it did this summer, they want nothing to do with it.

insights.claim: For investors wary of custody and security risk from hacks, lost wallets, or unreliable exchanges, buying a Bitcoin or Ethereum ETF through a mainstream brokerage such as Schwab or Fidelity removes direct custody risk versus holding tokens in a cold wallet or on a smaller exchange.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: ETFs are now a viable simplified access point that lowers the operational-risk bar to crypto exposure, relevant for advisors building diversified portfolios.
insights.quote: you can on most major brokerage firms buy an exchange traded fund that will just mirror Bitcoin or Ethereum or a number of these other tokens.

insights.claim: Crypto and stablecoin infrastructure is expected to become so normalized within about five years that today's conversation about whether to bother with it will feel as quaint as asking whether a business needs a website or an ATM card.
insights.speaker: Brett (Windrock Wealth Management)
insights.so_what: This normalization thesis implies the current adoption curve is still early, supporting a long-horizon allocation view despite near-term volatility.
insights.quote: I would not be shocked if in five years a lot of these things were norms and we'd look back and this conversation would be like, well, are you gonna have a website on the internet?
